Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old man with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, sore, red rash on chest, hands, and inner elbows; history of eczema; assessed as likely eczema flare. Plan: prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid, emollients for bath/shower, trial antihistamines (including fexofenadine), keep a trigger diary, and follow up in 7–10 days if not improving.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Very itchy, sore, red skin rash.
- Onset/duration: Began 4 days ago (doctor initially referenced 3 days; patient confirmed 4 days).
- Course/severity: Persistently severe itching; interfering with sleep and work concentration; limited hiking due to discomfort.
- Location: Chest, hands, and inside of elbows; no face involvement. Doctor later referred to chest and back (conflict noted).
- Character: Very itchy; skin is dry with some cracking; no bleeding or discharge.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: Daily showers provide some temporary relief; no known new triggers.
- Triggers/exposures: No clear trigger identified; patient does not recall changes in shower gel or clothing.
- Associated symptoms: Denies fever, cough, breathing difficulty, bowel or urinary issues.
- Prior episodes: History of eczema previously limited to arms; current episode more widespread and itchier.
- Treatments tried this episode: OTC “steroid cream” (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) purchased last night—no relief. Antihistamines recently—no relief (type/dose/frequency not documented).

Past Medical History:
- Eczema: Prior diagnosis; previously prescribed a cream and a shower/bath additive (details not documented); current flare more extensive and pruritic than prior episodes.
- Asthma: History in the past; patient reports no current asthma.
- No other chronic conditions reported.

Social History:
- Living situation: Lives with several flatmates to save money.
- Occupation: Full-time project manager at a pharmaceutical company.
- Tobacco: Does not smoke.
- Alcohol: A few beers per week; previously drank more when younger.

Family History:
- Not mentioned.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- General: Not documented.
- Skin: Clinician reports having viewed the rash; specific morphology/distribution details not documented.

Investigations:
- None discussed or performed.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Pruritic erythematous rash—likely eczema flare (atopic dermatitis)
  - Assessment details: 4-day history; severe pruritus and soreness; distribution chest/hands/antecubital fossae; cracked skin; no fever, discharge, or bleeding; prior eczema history; limited response to OTC steroid and antihistamines.
  - Plan:
    - Prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid (specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented).
    - Prescribe emollients for use in bath/shower; use regularly for 7–10 days.
    - Antihistamines: May use OTC loratadine or chlorphenamine (Piriton). Clinician also offered prescription fexofenadine (dose/frequency not documented).
    - Keep a diary of potential triggers (e.g., products, clothing); consider review if triggers identified.
    - Follow-up next week (7–10 days) if not improving.
- Issue 2: Sleep disturbance due to pruritus
  - Plan: Symptomatic control via above eczema management, including antihistamines.
- General plan items:
  - Return for reassessment if worsening, signs of infection (e.g., pus, spreading erythema, fever), or inadequate response.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: 
  - No vitals; no detailed skin exam description (morphology, extent, secondary infection signs); no photos; no specific medication names/doses/frequencies for prescribed steroid, emollients, or fexofenadine; allergies reviewed but only as “none.”
- Internal conflicts:
  - Onset documented as 3 days by clinician vs 4 days by patient; patient confirmed 4 days.
  - Distribution: Patient reports chest/hands/inner elbows; clinician later referenced chest and back—conflict noted.
  - Clinician addressed patient as “Sarah” once; patient presented as male—non-clinical identity mismatch noted.
- Transcript quality: Audio issues and intermittent clarity reported; some responses partially unclear.
